995.title: Traders, not armies
995.hook: Islam reached much of Southeast Asia through merchants and teachers
995.howItsDone: Muslim teaching on trade stresses honest weights, clear terms and keeping one's word, and in Southeast Asia, as elsewhere, Muslim traders may close their shops for Friday prayer and reopen afterward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aurangzeb and Dara Shikoh, and a hard history between two sons of the Taj's builder. Your line was: two brothers, two paths. What did you ask someone you disagree with? Day nine hundred ninety-five.

A ship sits in harbor on the coast of Sumatra, waiting for the wind to turn. It could be weeks. The merchants aboard can't sail home until the monsoon shifts, so they come ashore. They rent rooms, open shops, buy pepper, sell cloth. On Friday they find a quiet place and pray together. They make friends at the market. Some marry and stay. A teacher among them starts answering questions from curious neighbors. Nobody marches in. No banners. The new part of our path begins here: East and Southeast Asia. And it begins with people who came to sell things. Today: traders.
screen: `A SHIP WAITING FOR THE WIND.` → `SHOPS, FRIENDS, A FRIDAY PRAYER.` → `A NEW PART: EAST AND SOUTHEAST ASIA.`

segments.voice: Today, the call to prayer sounds across Indonesia and Malaysia. And yet, in much of the region, the faith did not arrive with a conquering army. It came along the trade routes of the Indian Ocean. Historians point to merchants from Arabia, Persia, India and China, and to Sufi teachers who traveled with them. It came slowly, port by port. Rulers of trading towns took up Islam, and their courts drew scholars. The traveler Ibn Battuta describes stopping at a port in Sumatra called Samudra and meeting its Muslim sultan, a ruler who loved to sit with scholars and debate. Why would merchants make good messengers? Partly because Islam has a lot to say about trade. Tradition remembers the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, as a merchant before his call. The Qur'an tells believers not to consume one another's wealth wrongly, but to trade by mutual consent. And of the Friday prayer it says, in Pickthall's translation: "And when the prayer is ended, then disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty." Prayer, then the market. A saying of the Prophet in Sahih al-Bukhari says that when buyer and seller are truthful and make things clear, their deal is blessed, and when they hide and lie, the blessing is wiped out. A merchant who weighs fairly, keeps his word, and closes the shop for prayer is a kind of sermon nobody has to preach. As the story is often told, neighbors watched how these traders lived before they listened to what they believed. Merchants carried it.
screen: `NOT WITH A CONQUERING ARMY.` · `PORT BY PORT, RULER BY RULER.` · `PRAYER, THEN THE MARKET.` · `TRUTHFUL TRADE IS BLESSED.` · then, large: `MERCHANTS CARRIED IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: trade honestly. Begin by looking at your own trades. Settle, and breathe. Think about the exchanges in your week: what you buy, what you sell, what you're paid for, what you promise. A job, a favor, a used bike online, a bill you're splitting. Is there one where you've been a little less than clear? A detail left out, a corner cut? Don't scold yourself. Just name it, and decide what clear would look like. If you pray, you can ask for honest hands. If you don't, simply decide. The bell holds the time.
Traders. The merchants and teachers who carried Islam along the sea routes to Southeast Asia, port by port, without an army. Today's word.
Your line: merchants carried it. Today, in one exchange, buying, selling or splitting a bill, be completely clear and fair, even where nobody would notice. Day nine hundred ninety-five.

996.title: Malacca on the straits
996.hook: a sultanate on the straits, a hub of trade and learning
996.howItsDone: In Malaysia, Malacca's history as a Muslim sultanate is taught as part of the country's story, and Malay is still written in Jawi script in some religious and traditional settings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, traders: merchants and teachers who carried Islam across the sea, port by port, with no army. Your line was: merchants carried it. Where were you completely clear and fair in a trade? Day nine hundred ninety-six.

A prince on the run is resting under a tree by a river mouth. His hunting dogs are out in the brush. Suddenly they corner a mouse-deer, a tiny, delicate animal. And the mouse-deer turns around and kicks one of the dogs straight into the river. The prince laughs, amazed. A place where even the smallest creature stands its ground, he says, is a good place for a city. He asks the name of the tree he's sitting under. It's a melaka tree. That's how the Malay Annals tell the city's beginning. Today: Malacca on the straits.
screen: `A PRINCE UNDER A TREE.` → `A MOUSE-DEER KICKS A DOG.` → `A CITY NAMED FOR THE TREE.`

segments.voice: Malacca sat on a narrow sea lane between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra: the Straits of Malacca. And it had something no fort can build: the winds. The monsoon blows one way for part of the year and the other way for the rest. Ships from India and Arabia came in on one wind, ships from China on the other, and both had to wait in port until the wind turned back. So Malacca became the place to wait, and to trade. Its rulers took up Islam, and took the Arabic title sultan. The Malay Annals tell this as a story too: the king dreams that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, teaches him the declaration of faith, and the next day a ship arrives carrying a scholar who leads the prayer, just as the dream foretold. Whatever happened, Malacca became a center not only of trade but of learning. Scholars and Sufi teachers came. The Malay language became a language of Islamic teaching and of commerce across the islands, written in an Arabic-based script called Jawi. Merchants from many lands lived in their own quarters, with their own heads, and dealt in pepper, cloth, spices, porcelain and gold. The Qur'an speaks of ships at sea as a sign: it says God made the sea of service, so ships could run on it and people could seek of His bounty, and give thanks. Malacca was built on exactly that. Later, Portuguese ships came and took the city, and the sultans moved on. But the language, the script and the faith had already traveled. The port of the straits.
screen: `A NARROW SEA LANE.` · `THE WINDS MADE IT A PORT.` · `A SULTAN, A DREAM, A SHIP.` · `MALAY IN JAWI LETTERS.` · then, large: `THE PORT OF THE STRAITS.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the straits on a map. If you have a phone nearby, find the Straits of Malacca between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra. If not, picture a long, narrow channel of sea between two green coasts. Settle, and breathe. Trace the water with your eyes or your finger, slowly, from the open ocean on one end to the other. Picture the ships at anchor, the languages on the docks, the call to prayer over the harbor. If you pray, you can pray for travelers at sea. If you don't, simply follow the water. The bell holds the time.
Malacca on the straits. A Malay sultanate on a narrow sea lane, where the winds brought ships from east and west, and trade and learning met. Today's word.
Your line: the port of the straits. Today, notice one busy place you pass through, a station, a store, a crowded street, and the many lives meeting there for a moment. Day nine hundred ninety-six.

997.title: The nine saints of Java
997.hook: nine saints remembered for teaching Islam through local arts and music
997.howItsDone: Javanese Muslims visit the graves of the Wali Songo as places of remembrance and prayer, and songs attributed to them, such as Tombo Ati, are still sung in homes, schools and mosques.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malacca, the port of the straits, where ships waited for the wind and traders, teachers and stories passed through. Where did you see something pass through a busy place yesterday? Day nine hundred ninety-seven.

Night on the island of Java. A white screen is stretched tight, a lamp burns behind it, and flat leather puppets throw long shadows across the cloth. An orchestra of bronze gongs and metal keys, the gamelan, rings and shimmers. A single puppeteer gives voice to kings, clowns and heroes until nearly dawn. Now a question. What would a teacher of a new faith do with a night like that? Ban it? Ignore it? Or step behind the screen and pick up a puppet? Javanese tradition has an answer, and it comes with nine names. Today: the Wali Songo.
screen: `A SCREEN, A LAMP, A PUPPET.` → `THE GAMELAN RINGS.` → `WHAT DOES A TEACHER DO?`

segments.voice: Wali Songo is usually rendered the nine saints. Wali is the Arabic word for a friend or close one of God; songo is the Javanese word for nine. Javanese tradition remembers these nine teachers as the ones who brought Islam deep into the island, and the stories about them share one thread: they did it by speaking the island's own language. The best-known story belongs to Sunan Kalijaga. Tradition says he took up the wayang, the shadow puppet play, and told its old tales in a way that carried new meaning, with the gamelan still ringing behind him. Another of the nine, Sunan Bonang, is remembered as a musician. A Javanese song called Tombo Ati, medicine for the heart, is attributed to him, and it is still sung today. Its verses name remedies for a troubled heart: reading the Qur'an and thinking on its meaning, prayer in the night, sitting with good people, fasting, and the long remembrance of God. A teaching, set to a tune people could carry home. Historians still argue over how much of these stories is history and how much is loving memory. Pilgrims still visit their graves. And the picture tradition keeps is clear. The Qur'an says: "Call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation." The nine saints, as Java remembers them, carried that wisdom in a tune the listener already knew. Not a new instrument. A new song on the old one. They taught with music.
screen: `WALI: A FRIEND OF GOD. SONGO: NINE.` · `KALIJAGA AND THE SHADOW PUPPETS.` · `BONANG AND THE MEDICINE FOR THE HEART.` · `WISDOM IN A TUNE PEOPLE KNEW.` · then, large: `CALL WITH WISDOM AND FAIR EXHORTATION.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one local song, beginning now with one you half know. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a song from where you live or where your family comes from. A lullaby, a street chant, a hymn, a folk tune, a football song. Find its first line. Hum it, quietly, under your breath. Notice what it carries besides the notes: a place, a person, a lesson someone wanted remembered. If you pray, you can let a word of remembrance ride on the tune. If not, just let it play. The bell holds the time.
Wali Songo. The nine saints of Java, remembered for teaching Islam through the island's own puppets, songs and gongs. Today's word.
Your line: they taught with music. Today, find the words of one local song you only half know, and learn the rest. Day nine hundred ninety-seven.

998.title: Indonesia, the largest
998.hook: the country with the most Muslims in the world
998.howItsDone: Indonesian Muslims pray in Arabic, often hear the Friday sermon in Indonesian or a local language, and students may study in pesantren or schools run by movements such as Nahdlatul Ulama and Muhammadiyah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Wali Songo, the nine saints of Java. Your line was: they taught with music. Did you find the rest of that half-known song? Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

Quick question. Where do the most Muslims on earth live? Not, by the usual count, in the lands of Arabic street signs. The answer lies far to the east, across an ocean, in a country of islands and volcanoes and rice terraces, where the street signs are in the Latin alphabet and the call to prayer drifts over palm trees and motorbikes. Java, where the nine saints taught, is one of its islands. Today: Indonesia.
screen: `WHERE DO THE MOST MUSLIMS LIVE?` → `NOT WHERE THE FIRST GUESS LANDS.` → `ISLANDS, VOLCANOES, RICE.`

segments.voice: Indonesia is usually counted as the country with the largest Muslim population in the world. And here is the surprise packed inside that line: the faith that arrived with traders and teachers didn't erase the islands' languages. It learned them. Indonesians speak many languages at home, and share one national language, Bahasa Indonesia, written in Latin letters. The prayers are in Arabic, the sermons are often in Indonesian, and the songs may be in Javanese or Sundanese or another of the island tongues. The Qur'an has a line for that: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours." Differences of language, in that verse, are not a problem to be solved. They are signs. Indonesia also holds its Muslims alongside neighbors of other faiths: Christians, Hindus in Bali, Buddhists, Confucians. Its national motto is in Old Javanese, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, usually rendered unity in diversity. Among Muslims there, two well-known movements stand out. Nahdlatul Ulama tends to keep the older customs of the pesantren, the village boarding school, and of visiting the graves of saints. Muhammadiyah, more of a reform movement, runs schools and hospitals and prefers a plainer practice. They differ, they argue, and both are deeply Indonesian. So when someone says the largest Muslim country, the number is only the doorway. Inside is a faith that speaks with many island accents.
screen: `THE LARGEST MUSLIM POPULATION.` · `ONE FAITH, MANY LANGUAGES.` · `THE DIFFERENCE OF YOUR LANGUAGES: A SIGN.` · `TWO MOVEMENTS, BOTH INDONESIAN.` · then, large: `THE LARGEST MUSLIM COUNTRY.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one Indonesian word. Here it is: terima kasih. It means thank you. Say it slowly: teh-REE-mah KAH-see. Settle, and breathe. On each out-breath, say it once, quietly. Then think of three people you could thank today, and give each of them your new word in your head. If you pray, you can thank God in whatever language you pray in. If not, let the thanks land on the people. The bell holds the time.
Indonesia. The island nation usually counted as home to more Muslims than any other, where one faith speaks in many languages. Today's word.
Your line: the largest muslim country. Today, say terima kasih once, out loud, to someone who helps you, and tell them what it means. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

999.title: Brunei and the Philippines
999.hook: Muslim sultanates of Borneo and Mindanao
999.howItsDone: In Brunei, Islam shapes public life and Malay is written in both Latin letters and Jawi; Muslims of the southern Philippines keep their own languages, sung epics such as the Darangen, and traditions from the old sultanates.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Indonesia, the largest Muslim country, and one faith speaking in many island languages. Did you get to say terima kasih to anyone? Day nine hundred ninety-nine.

A street sign in Brunei, on the island of Borneo. The name of the road is written twice. Once in Latin letters, the way Malay is usually written today. And once above it, in flowing Arabic letters. Same words, same language, two alphabets. That second script, Jawi, is Malay written in the letters of the Qur'an, and it is a small, daily clue to a bigger story. North and east of Borneo, across the sea, on the southern islands of the Philippines, there are clues like it. Today: Brunei and the Philippines.
screen: `A STREET SIGN IN BRUNEI.` → `ONE NAME, TWO ALPHABETS.` → `JAWI: MALAY IN ARABIC LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The trade winds that carried merchants to Malacca also carried them along the coasts of Borneo and up into the southern Philippine islands. Where trading towns took up Islam, local rulers often took a new title: sultan. On Borneo, the Sultanate of Brunei grew into a sea power along the coast, and it is still ruled by a sultan today, with Islam at the heart of public life and Jawi on its signs. Further north, on the islands of Sulu and Mindanao, the Sultanates of Sulu and Maguindanao rose and ruled the seas and rivers around them. Their Muslim peoples, the Tausug, the Maguindanao, the Maranao and others, are often called together the Moro. When Spain later took the northern islands, the southern sultanates resisted, and that history of struggle over land and self-rule runs long and hard, into modern times. Today much of the Muslim south forms the Bangsamoro autonomous region, within the Philippines. And there are stories. Around Lake Lanao, the Maranao people keep the Darangen, a long epic sung by performers, full of heroes, journeys, love and the old kingdom of Bembaran. It was sung at weddings and gatherings, holding up a people's memory of who they are. The Qur'an has a line about peoples and their differences: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Sultans, seas, an epic by a lake. The sultanates of the islands.
screen: `TRADE WINDS TO BORNEO AND THE ISLANDS.` · `BRUNEI: A SULTAN STILL REIGNS.` · `SULU, MAGUINDANAO, THE MORO.` · `THE DARANGEN BY LAKE LANAO.` · then, large: `THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one of their stories, starting with the shape of one. Settle, and breathe. An epic is a people remembering out loud. Think of one story your own family or town keeps telling: a journey, a hero, a loss, a wedding that went wrong. Run it through your mind slowly, the way a singer would. Then hold it next to the Darangen, sung by a lake far away. Different heroes, the same human need to remember. If you pray, you can ask for the good of the people of those islands. The bell holds the time.
Brunei and the Philippines. Sultanates of Borneo, Sulu and Mindanao, where Islam came by sea and sultans ruled the waters. Today's word.
Your line: the sultanates of the islands. Today, look up one Moro or Bruneian story, a scene from the Darangen or a tale from Sulu, and read it through. Day nine hundred ninety-nine.

1000.title: The Hui of China
1000.hook: Chinese-speaking Muslims whose ancestors came as traders and settled
1000.howItsDone: Hui Muslims pray in mosques called qingzhen si, keep halal kitchens marked qingzhen, and speak Chinese as their own language; Hui cooking, such as beef noodles and lamb dishes, is known across China.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sultanates of the islands: Brunei's Jawi street signs, the Moro of Sulu and Mindanao, the Darangen sung by Lake Lanao. Which island story did you find? Day one thousand.

A noodle shop on a busy street in a Chinese city. Steam on the windows. A cook slaps a rope of dough against the counter, stretches it, folds it, stretches it again, until it falls into the pot as a tangle of thin strands. The broth is beef. There's no pork anywhere in the kitchen. Above the door, two Chinese characters: qingzhen. The cook wears a small white cap. Everything here is Chinese, down to the chopsticks, and everything here is halal. Today: the Hui of China.
screen: `A NOODLE SHOP, STEAM ON THE GLASS.` → `NO PORK IN THE KITCHEN.` → `QINGZHEN ABOVE THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: The Hui are Muslims who speak Chinese as their own language. Their story, as Hui families and historians tell it, begins with traders: Arab and Persian merchants who came to China's ports by sea and its cities by the Silk Road, and later others from Central Asia. Some stayed. They married local women, raised children who spoke Chinese, and kept the prayer. Over generations the newcomers became neighbors, and the neighbors became a people. That is the heart of the Hui story. They don't have a separate homeland language or a far-off country to point to. They are Chinese, all the way through, and Muslim, all the way through. Their word for halal carries the same double belonging. Qingzhen is usually rendered pure and true. It is written over restaurants and butcher shops, and it is also used for a mosque, a qingzhen si, a temple of the pure and true. Hui scholars went further. Writers such as Wang Daiyu and Liu Zhi explained Islam in classical Chinese, using the vocabulary of Confucian learning, so that Chinese readers could meet the faith in their own philosophy. There is a saying people quote about this land, often attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: seek knowledge even as far as China. Hadith scholars have judged that saying weak, so it can't be leaned on as his words. But the Hui never needed it to belong. Their ancestors came, settled, and stayed. Chinese and Muslim.
screen: `TRADERS BY SEA AND SILK ROAD.` · `NEIGHBORS BECOME A PEOPLE.` · `QINGZHEN: PURE AND TRUE.` · `ISLAM IN CLASSICAL CHINESE.` · then, large: `CHINESE AND MUSLIM.`

segments.voice: The practice: try Chinese Muslim cooking, starting with a plan. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one dish: hand-pulled beef noodles, a lamb skewer with cumin, a sesame flatbread, a bowl of beef broth. Imagine the steps. Flour, water, salt, patience. Then think about where you could find it, or how you could make a simple version this week. Before you eat it, if you are Muslim, you can begin with bismillah. If you're not, you can simply notice the hands that made it. The bell holds the time.
The Hui of China. Chinese-speaking Muslims whose ancestors came as traders, settled, and became a people of their own. Today's word.
Your line: chinese and muslim. Today, look for a qingzhen or halal Chinese restaurant near you, or find one recipe for hand-pulled noodles and save it. Day one thousand.

1001.title: Xi'an's Great Mosque
1001.hook: a mosque built like a Chinese temple, with a pagoda minaret
1001.howItsDone: The Great Mosque of Xi'an is still a working mosque for the Hui community of the city's old Muslim quarter, who pray there facing west toward Mecca; visitors walk through its courtyards outside prayer times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hui of China. Your line was: chinese and muslim. Did you find a qingzhen kitchen, or a noodle recipe to save? Day one thousand one.

Step off a crowded lane in the old city of Xi'an, past stalls selling dates and lamb skewers, through a gate with a curved tiled roof. Inside: a garden courtyard. Stone tablets carved with Chinese characters. A carved wooden archway, painted and lacquered. Then another courtyard, and another, each quieter than the last. In the middle stands a tiered tower with upturned eaves like a pagoda. Everything says Chinese temple. And then, at the far end, people line up shoulder to shoulder, and someone calls Allahu akbar. Today: Xi'an's Great Mosque.
screen: `A GATE WITH A CURVED TILED ROOF.` → `COURTYARD AFTER COURTYARD.` → `A TOWER LIKE A PAGODA.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the Great Mosque of Xi'an goes back to the Tang dynasty; much of what stands today was built in later centuries. Either way, the builders made a choice. They didn't import a domed mosque from somewhere else. They built in the language of the place: courtyards laid out one after another, wooden halls on stone platforms, roofs of glazed tile. The tower in the courtyard serves as the minaret, but it looks like a pagoda pavilion, and its Chinese name speaks of examining the heart. Inside the prayer hall, the ceiling and wooden panels carry Arabic verses and Chinese decoration side by side, sometimes so blended that the Arabic letters curl like Chinese brushwork. One thing does not change with the clothes. The Qur'an tells the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: "So turn thy face toward the Inviolable Place of Worship." In Xi'an, that means west, toward Mecca, so the whole long line of courtyards runs east to west, and the prayer hall sits at the western end. Chinese walls, Chinese roofs, a Chinese garden, and a direction that points across the continent to the Ka'ba. Now look back at this week. Traders, not armies. The port of the straits. The nine saints who taught with music. Indonesia, one faith in many languages. The sultanates of the islands. The Hui, Chinese and Muslim. And this building, the whole week in wood and tile. A mosque in Chinese dress.

Walk slowly through the courtyards as they were described: the gate, the garden, the stone tablets, the tower, the long hall at the western end. Notice the direction you're walking. Then, when the bell ends, find a real photo of the Great Mosque of Xi'an and look at it slowly, the way you'd look at a face. Find one Arabic word, one Chinese roof, one place where they meet.
